text: Alright, who else thinks The Terminator is still the best sci fi action flick ever? That opening scene with the skeletal Terminator stomping through ruins, chills.
Dude yes, James Cameron basically invented the time loop thriller genre. Arnold Schwarzenegger as the T eight hundred, iconic. I'll be back is burned into my brain forever.
Don't sleep on Linda Hamilton though. Sarah Connor starts as this scared waitress and becomes a total badass by the end. Her transformation is wild.
When she's doing pull-ups in the psych ward in T2, you see the seeds here. But back to the original, Michael Biehn as Kyle Reese, underrated. His desperation sells the whole future war thing.
True, that scene where he's rambling about Skynet and the machines rising up in nineteen eighty four, you almost believe him even before the Terminator shows up.
Hammerin's pacing is insane. The truck chase through L A, the tech, gnar shootout, practical effects for the win. The stop motion Terminator skeleton, clunky but genius for the eighties.
Arnold's deadpan delivery kills me. Like, he's literally a robot, but you still feel weirdly scared of him. How'd they make a guy with a thick accent so emotionless?
Right, and the time paradox twist, Kyle Reese being John Connor's dad, mind blowing for nineteen eighty four. Sarah's whole choice speech at the end, goosebumps.
People forget how bleak it is. The ending with her driving toward the storm, recording those tapes, chills. No happy ending, just hope.
Cameron's genius was making you care about the humans more than the spectacle. Like, yeah, the Terminator's cool, but Sarah's arc, that's the heart.
Totally. Also, Paul Winfield as Lieutenant Traxler, that Terminator is out there, it can't be bargained with. Perfect delivery.
Think about the legacy too. Without Terminator, we wouldn't have Matrix, Westworld, anything with killer robots.
Still mad they never topped the first two sequels, but hey, at least this one's flawless. Sarah Connor forever.
Linda Hamilton deserves way more credit and shoutout to Stan Winston's creature design, those exposed hydraulics, timeless.
Yeah, absolutely. That pulsing synth score is so integral to the chase scenes. It's not just background music, it's practically a character itself.
Absolute masterpiece. Forty years later, and it still holds up. The Terminator is untouchable.
Alright, who else got their mind blown by Lawless again last night? Tom Hardy as Forrest Bondurant is next level. Dude barely speaks, but when he does, chills.

He stares down the corrupt cops with just a bottle of moonshine. Iconic. But let's not forget Gary Oldman as Floyd Banner. Man rolls up with a Tommy gun, blasting from his car window like a psychopath legend.
Oh, totally unhinged. But honestly, Guy Pearce's Charlie Rakes stole it for me. That greased hair, the creepy gloves, you could feel his slime through the screen. Hated him so much.
Ugh, yes, the way he tortured Shia La Beouf's Jack. Poor cricket, getting his hand smashed. I had to look away. But Jack's arc from the baby brother to stepping up. Shia killed it.
For real, the dynamic between the brothers felt raw. Howard's wild, drunk energy, Forrest's silent strength, and Jack's desperation to prove himself. That shootout in the woods, brutal.

John Hillcoat doesn't hold back the whole vibe, dusty thirties Virginia, the blood on the cornfields. It's like a Southern Gothic Western, and Jessica Chastain as Maggie, her quiet tension with Forrest added so much depth.
Speaking of anyone else obsessed with the soundtrack, that haunting folk music juxtaposed with violence, perfection. Felt like the land itself was a character, you know?
Absolutely, but let's talk about Mia Wasikowska as Bertha. Her scenes with Jack were sweet but tragic. You just knew their innocence wouldn't survive that world.
Yeah, the whole Wallis theme hits hard. The Bundren's thinking they're untouchable until the system crushes them. Until even Forrest admits, we're survivors chilling, not heroes.
And Floyd Banner's last stand, Gary Oldman chewing scenery while unloading bullets, campy but genius. Hillcoat walks that tone tightrope so well, you know.
Still, the real horror was Charlie Rakes. That final fight with Forrest, no music, just fists and grunts. Pearce and Hardy went feral. Oscar snub. Honestly.
Think it's underrated as a gangster flick. It's not Goodfellas glamour, it's dirt, family, and how far loyalty stretches. Also, Jack's narration's surprisingly poetic for a guy selling hooch.
Legends don't burn down shells every time.
Just finished rewatching Another Earth and man, that ending still messes with me. Brit Marling as Rhoda, so hauntingly good.

Write the way she plays guilt, written after crashing into John's family. William Mapother's performance too, when he stares at her cleaning his house, you feel the rage and grief without a single word.
And the whole Earth Two concept, genius. Mike Cahill's direction, using sci fi to explore regret and second chances. That shot of the duplicate planet hovering, chills.

Totally, but what gets me is the quiet moments, like Rhoda peeling wallpaper while John plays piano. It's so raw. Did you catch how their roles reverse? She becomes his caretaker, but he's still broken.
Yeah, and the radio contest subplot. When Rhoda wins the trip to Earth Two but gives it to John, that gut punch line. Maybe the other me didn't ruin your life.

I didn't stop. I just... kept driving. I didn't even know what I was doing. My hands were on the wheel, but I wasn't... I wasn't really there. I just kept going. I didn't know what else to do. I didn't know what to think. I just kept driving. I didn't know what else to do. I didn't know what to think. I just kept driving.
Mike Cahill loves blending realism with surrealism, like the scene where John's listening to space static and you hear whispers. Creepy but beautiful, right?
Think Earth two's actually a metaphor, like it's not literal, just their chance to forgive each other.
Whoa, never thought of that. But the final shot, Rhoda meeting her double, makes you wonder. Is that hope, or just another prison?
Either way, the emotional climax when they hug, waterworks. Twenty eleven Sundance Film Festival was right to honor it, such an indie gem.
Still mad it didn't get more awards. The soundtrack too, those eerie violin layers, perfectly unsettling.
True, but honestly I am just glad movies like this exist. Makes you stare at the sky differently.
Okay, who else still gets emotional when Remy finally gets to cook in Ratatouille? That tiny rat chef owns my heart. He's so.

Dude, the scene where he's controlling Linguini's movements by pulling his hair, genius animation. Patton Oswalt's voice acting for Remy is so full of passion, like you feel his obsession with flavors, man.

Right, and Linguini's whole arc from bumbling dishwasher to star chef is low key hilarious. Lou Romano nailed that awkward charm, but let's not forget Ian Holm as Skinner. That guy's villainous greed was spicy.

Skinner's obsession with exploiting the Gusteau name was wild. The frozen food empire? Classic corporate villainy. But Brad Bird's direction, man, balancing slapstick with deep themes about art and belonging? Chef's kiss.
Speaking of themes, Anton Ego's monologue about criticism, not everyone can become a great artist, but a great artist can come from anywhere, chills every time.

Peter O'Toole voicing Ego was P R E F E C T I O N. That cold intro where he walks into the restaurant like a vampire, iconic. And his redemption when he tastes the ratatouille, cuisine's best twist ever.
True, but can we talk about Colette? The only female chef in that toxic kitchen, kicking butt. You never hesitate. Her tough love training with linguine was everything.

Colette's motorcycle entrance though, total badass. But back to Remy, how brave was it for Pixar to make a rat the hero? The kitchen hygiene panic felt so real, but they made him adorable. I loved it.
My mom still side eyes me for loving a rat movie, but that finale where Ego writes his glowing review proves art transcends prejudice. Also, the actual ratatouille dish looked so simple yet magical.
Simple. That dish took months to animate. They studied real food obsessively. Fun fact, the team cooked real Ratatouille daily to get the lighting right. Dedication.
Worth it. That movie made me believe a rat could cook better than me. And Linguini's flailing dance when he's cooking, comedy gold. But low key, Skinner's tiny car chases were the unsung heroes.
Brad Bird's whole vibe, he did The Incredibles too, right? Man knows how to mix heart with spectacle. Also, the ending where Ego's review saves the restaurant? Best critic redemption arc ever.
Still mad Gusteau's ghost wasn't real, though. Anyone can cook hits harder when it's metaphorical. Okay, final take. Best Pixar food scene. The cheese and strawberry moment. Fight me.
Alright, who else just rewatched Rambo from two thousand eight? That finale with the machine gun, insane.
Oh my god, yes. Sylvester Stallone directing A N D starring. Talk about a one man powerhouse. But man, the violence in this one way gnarlier than the earlier movies.

Rambo moved through the jungle like a ghost, his machete catching the dappled sunlight as he approached the camp. The air was thick with humidity and the smell of damp earth. He stepped over a fallen log, his boots sinking slightly into the soft ground. Ahead, the camp was alive with activity—soldiers laughing around a fire, a radio crackling with static, a single machine gun mounted on a tripod, its barrel pointed toward the treeline.

Rambo didn’t hesitate. He lunged forward, the machete flashing in a wide arc. The first soldier barely had time to turn before the blade bit deep into his neck. Blood erupted in a crimson fountain, spraying across the dirt and the face of the man next to him. The practical effects were brutal—real blood, real flesh, real screams. The second soldier dropped his rifle and stumbled back, hands raised, but Rambo was already on him. The machete came down again, severing the man’s forearm. The severed limb hit the ground with a wet thud, twitching.

The turret gunner spun around, eyes wide with terror. He fumbled for the trigger, but Rambo was faster. He vaulted over the tripod, grabbed the gunner’s collar, and slammed his head into the metal frame. The man crumpled. Rambo didn’t stop. He grabbed the machine gun and turned it on the others. Bullets tore through canvas tents, splintering wood and sending men diving for cover. The practical effects were relentless—real smoke, real debris, real fear in the actors’ eyes.

One soldier tried to run. Rambo chased him through the underbrush, the machete raised. The man tripped over a root and fell. Rambo stood over him, breathing hard. The machete came down once, twice—then the man was still. The blood pooled around his head, dark and glistening in the jungle light.

Rambo stood there for a moment, breathing heavily. The camp was silent now, save for the crackle of the fire and the distant cry of a bird. He looked at the machine gun in his hands, then tossed it aside. He turned and disappeared into the trees, leaving behind a scene of carnage that felt too real to be anything but real.

I mean, that's the point. The Karen State massacre parallels. Salam said he wanted to expose the Burmese military's actual crimes. Julie Benz as Sarah broke my heart, though her begging Rambo to help.
For real, Sarah's the moral core. When she says, you didn't kill for your country, you killed for yourself. Oof, Stallone's face in that moment. Masterclass.
But let's not forget Matthew Marsden as Schoolboy. Dude's a sniper legend. His banter with Graham McTavish's Lewis, we're not saving the world, just our asses. Classic mercenary.
Louis's death though, stepped on a landmine. Mid sentence brutal, but Rambo's arc from recluse to vengeful warrior, peak character development.
Think Stallone overdid the gore, like the machete beheadings and kids forced into soldier camps. I get it's based on real atrocities, but damn.
Nah, it needed that rawness. The opening with the villagers being hunted, no music, just screams, chilling. Makes Rambo's rampage feel justified.
Plus, real Karen refugees were extras. Adds authenticity. But hey, anyone else notice the one take sequence when they stormed the camp? Camera follows Rambo nonstop. Genius directing.
Stallone's grunts alone deserve an Oscar. Dude's like sixty here. How's he still throwing punches like that?
Audunaleen and rage, man. That final scream into the jungle, haunting. He's not just a weapon anymore. He's human again.
Heavy stuff. Still, the ending credits with actual Burma footage. Gut punch reminder. It's not just a movie.
But does it romanticize violence to make a point like, here is the horror, now enjoy Rambo eviscerating fifty guys? Mixed messages.
Maybe. But the alternative was silence. At least it forced people to Google Karen State. Mission accomplished. Sly.
Did you guys catch that classic Phantom of the Opera remake from the forties? The one with Claude Rains? Man, his performance as the Phantom still gives me chills.

Oh yeah, the Arthur Lubin version. It's way darker than the musical adaptations. Susanna Foster as Christine totally stole the show with her operatic voice. That scene where she debuts as the lead soprano, chills.

Wait, but Claude Rains' transformation from sympathetic mentor to vengeful phantom is wild. Like, he literally disfigures himself after killing the publisher. The makeup effects were groundbreaking for nineteen forty three.

Honestly, Nelson Eddy has the baritone rival stealing Christine's spotlight low key annoyed me, but the opera house set's gorgeous. That chandelier scene where the phantom's shadow looms, pure gothic horror.
Right, Lubin nailed the atmosphere. But let's talk about Rameau's tragedy. Dude just wanted Christine to succeed. Then bam, accident, plagiarism, murder. His rage when he screams, my music haunts me.

Susanna Foster's chemistry with him though. When Christine realizes her mentor's the ghost, that mix of pity and terror, masterclass. Though why'd they cut the iconic mask from the original novel? Such a missed opportunity.
Budget or maybe Lubin wanted the Phantom's deformity to be more psychological. Rains acts so much with his eyes, you almost forget he's supposed to be hideous.
Still, the whole opera ghost myth feels way more tragic here. Like, he's not just a monster, he's a genius betrayed. That final scene where Christine tearfully sings as he disappears, gut punch.
Totally, and can we talk about Technicolor? For the forties, those reds and golds in the opera scenes were lush. Made Christine's rise to fame feel so mythic.
True, but the real star is the score. They use actual arias. When Christine hits that high C during Angel of Music, I get goosebumps. Susanna Foster was a legit opera singer, right?
Yep, fun fact. Rains hated singing. They dubbed his speaking voice over the Phantom's whispers. Creepy effect, though. Makes him sound like he's everywhere in the theater.
Classic Hollywood magic. Still, the moral's messy. Like, is the Phantom a villain or victim? Lubein leaves it ambiguous. I mean, he murders people, but you kinda root for his twisted love. It's wild.
That's why it's genius. No clean heroes or villains, just broken artists and stolen dreams. Way ahead of its time.
Alright, who else here just fell down the coffee and cigarettes rabbit hole? I can't stop thinking about those weird little conversations.
Oh totally, the Roberto Benigni and Stephen Wright bit killed me. Two legends just vibing, but like awkwardly. We love coffee, we love cigarettes, mocking their accents, so random.
Random but genius. Did y'all know the Iggy Pop and Tom Waits segment actually won the Palme d'Or for best short back in nineteen ninety three? Classic Jim Jarmusch. Absurd but profound.

Jim Jarmusch is the king of nothing happens but everything happens. That scene where Iggy's bragging about quitting smoking while smoking, peak irony. Tom Waits side eyeing him the whole time, iconic.

Right, and what about the twins ignoring that chatty waiter? That poor guy just wanted to bond over whatever, but they're just sipping coffee, blowing smoke, so uncomfortable. But I couldn't look away.
Jarmusch loves making us sit in that discomfort, like, why is everything in black and white? Feels like these conversations are stuck in some timeless limbo.
Exactly, the monochrome makes the coffee cups and cigarette smoke pop. It's all about texture, you know. No fancy C G I or sets, just people, vices and awkward silences.
Speaking of people, Xinke Li and Jui Li as the twins, underrated. Their deadpan stares could cut glass, make you wonder if Jarmusch told them, just exist, but make it existential.
Lab. Existential is the word. Even the segment with the two old guys drinking instant coffee at midnight. It's like, is this about loneliness, connection, or just caffeine addiction?
Both. The whole film's a Rorschach test. Like, when Roberto Benigni keeps nervously relighting his cigarette, is it comedy or tragedy? Stephen Wright's monotone doesn't help.
Jarmusch's casting, though. Musicians, comedians, indie icons. It's a who's who of cool. But the dialogue's so stiff it loops back to being poetic. Coffee's a metaphor. No, it's just coffee.
Classic, you either love his vibe or hate it. Me, I am obsessed. It's like a Levantine play about human connection failing spectacularly, and everyone's too polite to leave.
Politeness is the real villain. Pass the coffee. Avoid eye contact. Keep smoking. Honestly, mood.
Alright, who else thought Sherlock Holmes was way funnier than it had any right to be? James Mc Avoy as No Mayo kills me every time.
Oh totally, his banter with Emily Blunt's Juliet, adorable but Johnny Depp as Sherlock Gnomes stole the show, that raspy dramatic voice, pure Depp magic.
For real though, Chiwetel Ejiofor as Watson was low key genius. The way he deadpans Sherlock's over the top theories, elementary my dear, no mayo, iconic.
Wait, did y'all catch that? This was directed by John Stevenson, same guy who did Kung Fu Panda. Explains the wild mix of slapstick and heart.

True, the London adventure vibe was cool, but the kidnapping plot got dark fast. All those gnomes vanishing, Gnomeo's panic when his crew goes missing. James Mc Avoy nailed that mix of comedy and desperation.
Right, and Juliet, being the voice of reason, we're garden gnomes, not detectives. But her teaming up with Sherlock anyway, growth, I guess.
Speaking of Sherlock's gadget obsession, the tiny magnifying glass, hilarious, but Watson carrying him emotionally, underrated duo.
Don't forget the new characters. That flamingo statue with the attitude. Darling, this is London. I died.
The whole city exploration angle was smart. Showing Narnia sized London through sewers and flower pots. Clever world building.
But the real M V P was the soundtrack, Elton John bangers remixed with Gnome puns, Tiny Dancer, chef's kiss.
Okay, but the villain twist didn't see that coming. The spoiler being behind the kidnappings, legit shocking. What do you think?
Right, and Sherlock's redemption arc, learning to trust others, way deeper than I expected from a gnome movie.
Still, the best part was Naomi and Juliet's dynamic. They're so chaotic together. We're not just garden decorations.
Hundred percent that final battle where they rally all the garden ornaments. Pure chaos. I was cheering.
Think they'll make a third one, Romeo and Juliet versus Alien Lawn Mowers?
Stop it, they totally do that.
Alright, who else just binged Striking Distance last night? Bruce Willis as Tom Hardy, classic nineties cop drama gold.
Oh totally, that river chase scene with the Pittsburgh skyline insane, but Sarah Jessica Parker as Joe totally stole it for me. Her sarcasm balanced Willis' brooding.
Nah, Dennis Farina as Uncle Vince was the MVP. You are a mess, Tommy. That line lives rent free in my head. But Chris, you really think the killer twist was obvious?
Hold up, Marcus, Tom sees more. Eddie being the mole and connected to Tom's dad's death. I didn't see that coming. Director Roddy Harrington layered those clues so subtly.
Right, the whole cop killing cops angle got me when Tom finds his dad's old badge in Eddie's apartment. Chills. Bruce Willis nailed that rage grief combo.
But let's talk about the emotional baggage, Tom blaming himself for Vincent's death. The scene where he smashes the evidence room mirror, that's peak Willis intensity.
True, but the romance subplot with Joe felt rushed. Like, they're arguing about case files one minute, then kissing in the rain the next. Come on, Roddy, really?
Disagree. Their tension built naturally. Joe calling him out, You are not the only one with ghosts. Hardy Parker delivered that line like a dagger. Perfection.
Back to the villain, Eddie's smugness when he taunts Tom, your daddy knew too much. Seymour played unhinged so well, shame he didn't get more recognition for this role.
Also the soundtrack, that grunge rock vibe, screaming nineties thriller, chef's kiss. But Marcus, you really called the twist early.
Okay, maybe obvious was harsh, but the second time they showed the killer's gloves, I guessed it was someone internal. Still, the dart connection gut punched me.
Exactly, that's what elevates it from generic thriller to a tragedy about legacy. Tom avenging Vincent while becoming him, full circle poetry. Roddy Harrington doesn't get enough credit, man.
Hundred percent this and Die Hard proved Bruce Willis owned the nineties. Who's up for a double feature next week?
Just finished rewatching Spotlight for like the fifth time. Man, that scene where Mark Ruffalo's character Mike snaps in the office, they knew and they let it happen. Chills every single time.
Oh my god, yes. Michael Keaton as Robbie Robinson is so understated but powerful when he's arguing with Liev Schreiber's Marty Baron about taking on the whole church. You can feel the tension.
And Rachel McAdams as Sasha Fierz interviewing survivors, the way she balances empathy with journalistic rigor, it's masterclass acting. Did you guys know the real Sasha consulted with her?
No way, that explains the authenticity. Tom McCarthy's direction is so unflashy, right? Like no dramatic music, just close ups of their faces as they realize it's not just a few bad priests.

Exactly, the moment they tallied up the eighty seven priests in Boston alone, my jaw dropped and the church's lawyers just shrugging it off like, what, you never heard of confidentiality? Infuriating.

What gets me is how systemic it was, like, the cops, the judges, everyone complicit. That scene where the old lawyer says, if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. Haunting.
And the Globe's own role in ignoring the story earlier, brutal self critique, makes you wonder how many modern institutions are hiding their own spotlight.
Totally, it's not just a period piece, it's a manual for investigative journalism. The way they cross reference directories and church transfers, mundane but thrilling.
Still can't believe it, lost best picture to Birdman. Wait, no, Michael Keaton was in both. Talk about irony.
Harsh, but Spotlight's legacy is bigger than Oscars. Real life impact: survivors getting validation, the church reforms. That's the win.
True, that final scroll listing all the cities with abuse cases, gut punch makes you wanna go hug a journalist.
Or become one, afflict the comfortable and comfort the afflicted, right?
Dude, I just rewatched Stay Alive last night and it's still creepy as hell. How did John Foster's character even think playing that cursed game was a good idea?
Right, William Brent Bell really knows how to blend horror with tech. Remember when Hutch started seeing Elizabeth Báthory's ghost in his apartment? I nearly threw popcorn at the screen.
Okay, but Frankie Muniz as Swink, that guy's performance was low key terrifying when he screamed, it's not a game anymore, chills, man, actual chills.
Can we talk about the real life history though? Elizabeth Bathory, the Bloody Countess, bathing in blood? The game's lore was way darker than I expected. How'd they even tie that to a video game?
Shoutout to Samara Armstrong as Abigail, though her death scene with the spider webs, brutal. I read they used practical effects for that, no C G I.
Wait, didn't Milo Ventimiglia's character die in the first act? Like, the whole passing the game to your friend trope. Classic horror setup, but Bell made it feel fresh. What do you think?
Fresh more like traumatizing Jimmy Simpson as Phineas deserved. Better man, dude just wanted to hack the game, not get stabbed by a ghostly noblewoman. Shame.
True, but the stakes felt real. Once the game memorizes your face, you were done, no reset button. That scene where they're all screaming, stay alive, while the credits rolled. Iconic.
Still, why'd Hutch keep playing after his friend died? Pride, stupidity. John Foster nailed that desperate gamer vibe though.
Mix of both, probably. But the real horror is how the game morphs reality, like Elizabeth Bathory's portrait changing. Nope, I'd have yeeted that PlayStation out the window.
Playstation, please. It was totally an Xbox. But yeah, the whole survival horror genre owes this movie. Even if the reviews were mixed, it's a cult classic now.
Cool classic with historical flavor. I'm just saying if a friend hands me a game called Stay Alive, I'm burning it.
Alright, who else just finished Transit Camp? My mind's still stuck in that final scene with the burning letters.
Oh man, that movie's heavy. Tom Roberts doesn't hold back, does he? The way he frames those close ups on the prisoners' faces, it's like you can see their souls crumbling.
Vera Farmiga as Natalia, though, her performance when she confronts her husband's trauma, I felt that in my bones, the guilt, the desperation. She's a masterclass.
And Thomas Kretschmann as Colonel Virov, cold as ice. But that moment he lets Natalia keep her medikit, chills. You almost forget he's a P O W commander.
But let's talk about Daniel Brühl's Klaus. The scene where he admits he's not the S S officer they're hunting. The way his voice cracks, you realize he's just a kid who survived hell.
Right, and Natalie Press as Irina, the guard who softens toward Klaus. Their dynamic's so messed up but weirdly human, like Stockholm syndrome meets war exhaustion. You know what I mean?

Tom Roberts loves moral gray zones. Remember when General Pavlov, John Malkovich's character, orders Natalia to torture suspects? The camera lingers on her shaking hands. No music, just silence. Brutal.
Speaking of Makovich, his delivery of mercy is a luxury we burned in Stalingrad. Straight up villainy, but you get why he's broken. War corrupts everyone.
The cinematography too, all those bleak washed out colors. Even the barracks feel like tombs. Symbolic much?
Did anyone catch the historical nods, like the reference to the real life Soviet Order Number Forty Six, chilling accuracy.
Still the ending guts me. Natalia burning the list of suspects to protect Klaus and Irina, sacrificing her own freedom. Was it redemption or another tragedy?
But Roberts doesn't do neat endings. It's like he's saying war leaves everyone in limbo. No heroes, just survivors.
And Vera's last line: We're all ghosts here, shaped to the camp's empty watchtowers. Yeah, I am not sleeping tonight.
Alright, who's still emotionally recovering from If Beale Street Could Talk? Barry Jenkins doesn't miss, man.
Ugh, me. That opening montage of Fanny and Tish in Harlem. The colors, the music. It's like poetry. Kiki Lane's face tells the whole story without words.
Right, and Stephan James is funny the way he balances anger and vulnerability. When he's screaming in the prison phone booth, shattered me.
Don't even get me started on Regina King as Sharon. Her trip to Puerto Rico to find that witness. The quiet rage in her eyes. She earned that Oscar. Period.
Barry Jenkins close ups though. Like when Tish tells Fonny she's pregnant. The camera lingers on their hands touching through the glass. Genius.
The seventies Harlem vibe is so immense, the jazz score, the fashion, but man, the injustice hits hard upon his arrest scene, straight up gut punch.
And Coleman Domingo as Mister Rivers, his speech about fighting with love instead of fists, that's the heart of the film. Systemic racism bases black joy.
Real talk, Tisha's voiceovers killed me. I hope nobody ever loves you as much as I love him. Like, how do you even breathe after that line?
But the ending bittersweet perfection, Fonny out on parole, holding his son, but you know the system's still lurking. It's not fair.
True, but Barry Jenkins isn't about neat endings. It's about love surviving anyway. That final shot of young Chiron and Kevin dancing, tears for days.
Also, can we talk about how this is Jenkins' follow up to Moonlight? Dude's obsessed with intimacy under pressure. Masterclass in restraint.
Totally, the dinner scene where both families argue about the baby, the tension, but then Sharon slams the table, chef's kiss, Regina King forever.
Still mad it didn't win best picture. That movie's a time capsule of Black love and resilience. More people need to see it.
Just rewatched Desert Hearts for the third time and I am still not over that rain scene. Patricia Charbonneau as Cay, absolute legend.
Oh man, the tension between her and Helen Shaver's Vivian. When Kay says, I don't want to be your experiment, I felt that in my bones.

Right, and this was made in the nineteen eighties. Donna Deitch really said, let's make a lesbian romance that's actually tender and de steamy. The way she frames their eye contact in the casino chef's kiss, it's like.

Can we talk about the historical context? Vivian's whole divorce struggle in nineteen fifties Nevada. Imagine needing to live on a ranch for six weeks just to file papers. Frankie's ranch felt like its own character.
Helen Shaver's performance, though, the subtlety, like when Vivian hesitates to touch Kay's hair after the car ride, you see her entire internal battle in one glance.
And Kay's confidence masking her vulnerability. I am twenty five. I am not harmless. Charboneau delivered that line like a velvet punch.
The fact that this was adapted from Jane Rule's novel, the dialogue's so sharp, you are the first thing that's ever happened to me. I didn't plan, of my heart.
It's wild this was made for three hundred and fifty thousand dollars. That train station ending with them holding hands. Simple, revolutionary.
The humor too. Kay's cowboy hat swagger versus Vivian's buttoned up blouses and Frances, the stepmom, lowkey shipping them while watering plants. Iconic.
Francis was a whole mood. You think I don't know what's going on here, ma'am? You are the O G ally.
This film's legacy, though, first mainstream lesbian love story to get wide distribution. No tragic endings, just two women choosing joy. Nineteen eighty five needed that.
Still holds up that scene where Kay teaches Vivian to dance. No words, just the radio and desire. Donna Deitch knew exactly when to let silence speak.
Alright, who else thought My Spy was way funnier than it had any right to be? Dave Bautista as this grumpy spy getting outsmarted by a kid genius, it was gold.
Yes, Chloe Coleman as Sophie stole the whole movie. That scene where she blackmails him by threatening to post his undercover photos, I'll hashtag your face, I died.

Dave's comedic timing is underrated, man. Like when he tries to act normal at the school pickup. Dude looked like a bear wearing a dad costume. And Kristen Schaal as Bobby, his tech partner, her panic attacks over the mission going sideways so awkwardly hilarious.

But it's not just slapstick, right? The whole fake dad bonding thing got me when Sophie sets him up with her mom, Perissa Fitzhenley's character, and he's suddenly teaching her self defense. Unexpectedly sweet.

Totally, Director Peter Segal nailed that balance. Like, the action scenes are decent but the heart's in the weird family dynamic. Did y'all catch Ken Jeong's cameo as the neighbor? Is this a midlife crisis or a spy thing? Legendary.
Chloe Coleman deserves awards. Period. How does a kid actor pull off sassy and vulnerable in the same breath? That moment she calls him out for lying about her dad, oof.
Dave's growth from lone wolf to actually caring. Chef's kiss. Reminded me of Guardians of the Galaxy, but with more juice boxes.

And can we talk about the script? Sophie making him do TikTok dances as part of the blackmail peak comedy. But also real talk, the movie low key addresses single parent struggles. Kate working doubles while Sophie feels lonely. It's hard, you know.
True, it's a spy comedy with layers. Even the villain subplot generic, sure, but who cares when the chemistry's this good?
Also, fun fact, Day's real life daughter played a little girl in the park scene. He talked about it in an interview. Makes the dad deeds even sweeter.
No way, okay, new appreciation, but let's be real, best part was the bloopers during credits, Dave cracking up while Chloe roasts his wrestling moves, gold.

Alright, who else thinks Baby Mama is low key one of the most underrated comedies from the two thousands? Tina Fey and Amy Poehler together, gold ass.
YES their chemistry is insane like when Amy Poehler's character Angie fakes the insemination syringe squirt I died laughing how is that scene not iconic

Okay, so I finally watched The Maplewood Murders last night. Charles Palmer really nailed that classic Agatha Christie vibe, didn't he?
Oh totally, Geraldine McEwan as Miss Marple is perfection. The way she notices everything with those piercing blue eyes, chills. So good.
Right, and Rachel Sterling as Lettice Protheroe, such a complex role. You never know if she's grieving her father or secretly relieved he's gone.
Oh, that scene where she confronts Reverend Clement. Janet Mc Teer's reaction was priceless. You'll regret those words, Colonel. So much tension.
Don't even get me started on Jason Flemyng's Inspector Slack. His constant head butting with Miss Marple. Classic. This isn't a knitting circle, madam.
But let's talk about the actual murder. Prothero had like a dozen enemies. I totally thought it was the vicar's wife until the third act twist.
Same. Charles Palmer dropped those red herrings like breadcrumbs. And the vicarage set design, so cozy yet sinister, felt like nineteen thirties England. Chilling.
Geraldine's monologue about human nature after the arrest. Evil thrives when good people knit too quietly. Iconic.
Honestly, the whole cast killed it. But can we appreciate how Palmer balanced humor with the grim stuff like the tea party right after the body was found?
Yes, darkly hilarious. Also, did you catch that Miss Marple never leaves the village? Her whole world's a microcosm of human vice. Genius.
Still can't believe Preverro was shot in broad daylight with six suspects nearby. That's a brazen killer.
Or a desperate one. Palmer makes you sympathize with the murderer by the end, which is wild. Miss Marple's quiet empathy does it again.
Exactly, it's not just a who done it, it's about why. Mc Ewan's subtlety there, Oscar worthy honestly.
Think they'll adapt more Miss Marple mysteries with this cast. I need Rachel Stirling in more period dresses stat.
If they do, Charles Palmer better direct. This one's a masterclass in cozy crime.
Dude, I finally watched Wishmaster last night. How have I slept on this nineties horror gem? Andrew Divoff as the Djinn is pure nightmare fuel.

Write that voice smooth but somehow rotting from the inside when he purrs, make your first wish. Chills tumble Lauren as Alexandra holds her own, though her panic feels so real when she realizes the three wishes rule.

Robert Kurtzman directed it, right? The guy who did all those killer special effects in Evil Dead. You can tell the body horror scenes, like that melting face in the museum prologue. Practical effects for days.
Oh God, the skeletonization scene. But let's talk about Robert Englund's cameo as the shady merchant. Best five minutes ever. The Djinn is not some genie in a lamp. So campy, but genius.

Y'all sleeping on the mythology. Ancient Persia stuff with the trapped jinn, the ruby prison, smart how they tied it to real Arabic folklore. But why do people keep making third wishes? Alexandria should've googled evil genie loopholes. That's the real issue.
Because horror logic, Jake. But De Vos' performance elevates it. When he morphs into different characters to trick people, that bartender disguise was slick.
True, but Wendy Benson as the sister deserved more screen time. Her death by gold seemed brutal, like, imagine wishing for wealth and literally choking on molten coins.
Classic monkey's paw twist. My favorite was the lawyer who wished to live forever, turned into a screaming mummy statue. Kurtzman loves his ironic punishments.
Think it's scarier than modern C G I fads. That rubbery gin true form holds up, and the way it ties into that opening curse from the eleventh century. Full circle storytelling.
Still mad t here is no sequel where the Djinn invades Times Square or something. But nah, the ending with Alexandra smashing the Ruby Perfection Sacrifice one hundred and one.
Hold up, did anyone catch the Tales from the Crypt? The gin's like R rated Crypt Keeper, even the color palette screams late nineties anthology horror.
Hundred percent, it's a love letter to E C comics, but modern audiences would whine about pacing their loss. More gin monologues for us.
